Un excellent rogue-lite qui mélange livre dont vous êtes le héro, tarot, gestion des ressources, combats dynamiques et intrigues. Avoir jouer au 1 n'est pas obligatoire même si je vous le conseille pour apprécier encore plus à quel pour cet opus est une amélioration de ce dernier.

Positif :
+ ambiance incroyable, maitre du jeu mémorable et vrai sensation de réussite quand on bat un défi
+ toutes les mécaniques du 1 ont été raffinées et poussées plus loin
+ le jeu est dur mais tout à fait faisable avec de l'entrainement et de la stratégie (et un brin de chance)
+ la structure en "petites histoires" des cartes pousse à vouloir tout découvrir, même si le gain qu'elle ne nous intéresse pas


Négatif : que dans le détail !
- certaines énigmes/challenges sont trop vagues ou spécifiques et demande un wiki ou beaucoup d'essais
- assez rapidement, la difficulté croissante pousse à ne pas choisir trop de cartes inconnues et privilégier les "valeurs sûres". Combiné au nombre importante de cartes débloquables, il est nécessaire de farmer des missions en boucle ou jouer en mode infini pour obtenir les jetons/fragments car un run normal de toutes missions ne suffit clairement pas.
- le combat est difficile à première vue puis trivial une fois maîtrisé, bien qu'un peu brouillon (sélection de cible, coups parfois discutables qui nous touchent...)
- les mini-jeux de tirage sont très difficiles et parfois assez inégaux dans leur part de chance/maitrise et d'équipements dédiés pouvant nous faciliter la tâche
- niveau final assez décevant, même si ceux qui le précédent font office de climax suffisant en soit

If you thought the first game was special, Hand of Fate 2 somehow raises the stakes in every possible way.

From the very first challenge, the sequel feels bigger, bolder, and far more ambitious. The deck-building adventure returns, but this time with more structured scenarios, companion characters, and narrative choices that give each run a stronger sense of purpose. Every card you add to your deck isn’t just content, it’s a statement about how you want your journey to unfold. The gameplay loop remains incredibly satisfying: build your deck, face the Dealer, adapt to the unexpected, and slowly master the chaos.

What truly stands out again is the atmosphere. Sitting across from the Dealer still carries that same theatrical tension, but this time there’s a sharper edge to the rivalry. Antony Skordi once again delivers a phenomenal performance. His voice gives the Dealer an even greater sense of presence and personality, elevating every encounter with subtle mockery, menace, and grudging respect as you grow stronger. He doesn’t just oversee the game, he feels like an active opponent.

Combat is tighter and more refined, expanding on the Arkham-inspired rhythm with new enemy types, weapons, and companions that genuinely change how encounters play out. The added mechanics make fights feel more dynamic, while the card-based structure ensures no two runs unfold the same way.

Hand of Fate 2 doesn’t just repeat the formula, it evolves it. It’s one of the most creative and distinctive roguelike experiences out there, and in many ways, it perfects what made the original so memorable.

This is a good game, however, what you get out of it will vary on your tolerance for RNG mechanics. The game is a roguelike deck building game with action combat, player choice,  and a lot of text. The writing is good so if you do not mind reading a lot you will find it engaging.

There are over 20 campaign scenarios including additional challenges and an endless mode. Each story is unique and well written with a lot of interesting scenarios and outcomes that you build out of the cards you collect. The narrator is one of my favorite parts of the game and the story revolves around you sitting in his wagon as he deals the cards to your adventure. His personality and dialogue is interesting, and I liked hearing what he has to say out of every interaction within the game.

The further you get the more cards you unlock which add onto your equipment, items, story opportunities, etc. The game has a heavy focus on RNG so you play a lot of 'chance' games such as throwing dice and picking the correct card. There is a lot of frustration in the later campaigns but when things go your way it is a nice feeling. 

Your first impression may be that the game is easy but as you progress towards the later levels you will realize just how difficult it gets. It will get to the point where you think it is unfair and want to uninstall it. I think that is part of the fun though and it makes the good outcomes all the more rewarding.

My least favorite aspect is the combat because it gets tiring. It is not that deep and when there are a lot of enemies in such a small arena it gets difficult to manage. The campaigns that are combat heavy are the ones that I like the least. I just want to get the fight over with so I can get back to the story that is unfolding. 

If the premise of the game sounds interesting then I think you will enjoy it.

Text Review:

Pros:
-Great card and roguelike elements with a whole lot of tokens to unlock (And thus cards) and this keeps it rewarding and the carriage gaming table set-up with all its gambits and gaming paraphernalia is a lovely thing to base a game around
-Good story and world-building (Some quests are excuses for content but the encounters are descriptive and well written. You read so much it's almost like a visual novel. Companion quests can make you care about them but I believe the main plot has some mishaps and later you will skip some of the interchangeable quest descriptions as you pick them multiple times out of proficiency - once read they become tools)
-Nice string-heavy musical and audio ques that give a lovely gaming atmosphere as well as one of the mysterious and mystic (Breathes life into the card game that some may argue isn't supposed to be that interesting but I didn't really register the combat music so I guess it was OK)
-The Dealer's voice over work is nice but there isn't much voice over work in general

Maybes:
-Visually mixed bag (Graphics are decent but it has a bland feel with limited character customization, mass use of the same enemy model, a lot of greyish/ yellow for the cards and brown in the carriage, the physics and animations are a bit unrefined, great gaming table with all the paraphenalia and their use of bright, radiating, blueish silver cards for powerful platinum cards and burning orange for the harder brimstone cards made for a nice old timey take on holographic cards)
-Game does involve a bit of luck but it's not that hard to stack things in your favor and some of the gambits are skill based
-The fact that the tokens (And thus new cards) are more fun to pursue than the main quest encourages farming for them (Perhaps on a level you've already completed) and it's annoying if after all that effort you fail or simply if the token targets are massive, vague or hard

Cons:
-The combat is simple and can feel like busy work when the fights are so repetitive with large groups of the same enemies that don't really overwhelm you - They attack one at atime and you can interupt your own attack to press counter when they attack. It's not hard and even though the weapons have stats I rarely had to look at them... I could choose equipment for whom I still needed to unlock the token regardless of how strong it was a lot of times (It is fun though: A watered down version of the Arkham/ Assassin's Creed system of dodges, counters etc.)

This a very good one-shot game, if you enjoy an immersive, fourth-wall-breaking deck builder with a big parts of fantasy combat elements. It also has some puzzles in it. The dialogues (on encounter cards) are not tediously long to read. If you liked HoF1 and don't know about the DLCs in HoF2, get it in a bundle, it's worth it.

You build a deck consisting of encounters and equipment, you play the deck. The story and sub-stories of single cards progress as you visit those cards. The RNG is very strong with this, as it should. You can get incredible runs (within your available/unlocked card's limits) or you can have the worst runs and encounter big bosses on the first dice roll without any gear. But you can always restart a run without punishments. In extreme cases your only punishment will be some time waste because of bad luck RNG, which is bearable.

Towards the end, the game can get a very grindy if you're after all unlocks and achievements, but honestly it's kind of not worth it. Still a great game, enjoyed every bit of it! It has an endless mode too, which i tried, but there wasn't much new stuff to discover.

Hand of Fate 1 is equally great, but 2 is better in some aspects. I'd recommend HoF1 then HoF2 though, because of the QoL and other Improvements you'll be missing if you play the wrong order.

When I started playing the game I was curiousm but I felt it was still "light" on it´s core gameplay... initially.

However, I have to say that I got hooked to finish it, and did it over a long time (the way I enjoy gaming :) )

Interesting formula of mixed mini-games that are triggered by event cards.
Cards are hidden in the board, and you reveal them one by one and solving each event before continue.

You navigate the board game of cards with a token/avatar of you, and solve those events with certain decisions or by winning/loosing the mini-games.
Your character relies on it´s health, food and money to survive each chapter and try to solve each one in different ways.
The objectives are different per chapter. 

There is a preparation phase where you select a companion, weapons, possible events to encounter and some specific resources. 
By solving each chapter you unlock further weapons, events, armor, items and more resources that can be used further on other chapters.
The minigames may include combat, dices, a pendulum to stop, traps, card tricks, etc
They are not very deep on their own, but they have interesting variations.  
Items make important differences when facing those mini-games to avoid falling into "pure luck" outcomes. 

The entire game is not very deep in complexity and the advantage of that is that you get it how to play early. 

The only downside that I can mention is that even if prepared with the adequate set of items/encounters you will fail sometimes against pure luck, but in the end is not that critical as you can recover over other encounters too.

The game increases difficulty by adding more limitations, curses, and punishing you in hard ways to make you fail at some point. 
For example the combat is not difficult to understand, but the game will put you many times with some stronger enemies in situations that maybe you are already hurt after some previous bad encounters. 
So it is a struggle many times, but well planned you can balance things much better. 

Therefore you may end up re-starting the chapters choosing better options, is ok.
